lessons.title: Predicting Chemical Reactions — Reactivity
lessons.description: Reactivity series, displacement reactions, and metal extraction using carbon.
lessons.content_html:
The Reactivity Series

Metals can be arranged in order of their reactivity series. The most reactive metals (such as potassium and sodium) are at the top, and the least reactive (such as gold and platinum) are at the bottom. The reactivity of a metal depends on how easily it forms a positive ion by losing its outer-shell electrons. Metals higher in the series lose electrons more readily because their outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner electron shells.

The order from most to least reactive is: potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, carbon, zinc, iron, hydrogen, copper, silver, gold, platinum. Carbon and hydrogen are included as reference points even though they are not metals — carbon’s position determines how metals can be extracted, and hydrogen’s position determines which metals react with dilute acids.

Key Fact

A metal’s reactivity depends on how easily it loses its outer electrons to form a positive ion. More reactive metals react more vigorously with water and dilute acids. The tendency to form positive ions increases up the reactivity series.

Reactions of Metals

You can deduce the reactivity of a metal from its reactions with water and dilute acids. Very reactive metals (K, Na, Li, Ca) react vigorously with cold water to produce a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas. For example, sodium reacts with water: \(2Na(s) + 2H_2O(l) \rightarrow 2NaOH(aq) + H_2(g)\). Calcium reacts more gently, producing a cloudy solution as calcium hydroxide is only slightly soluble.

Moderately reactive metals (Mg, Zn, Fe) react very slowly or not at all with cold water but react well with dilute acids to produce a salt and hydrogen gas. For example, magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid: \(Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) \rightarrow MgCl_2(aq) + H_2(g)\). Unreactive metals (Cu, Ag, Au) do not react with water or dilute acids because they do not lose their electrons easily enough.

Displacement Reactions

A displacement reaction occurs when a more reactive metal replaces a less reactive metal from a compound. For example, if you place iron in copper sulfate solution, the iron displaces the copper:

$$Fe(s) + CuSO_4(aq) \rightarrow FeSO_4(aq) + Cu(s)$$

The iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces it. The blue copper sulfate solution turns colourless (iron sulfate) and a brown coating of copper appears on the iron. A less reactive metal cannot displace a more reactive one — copper in iron sulfate solution would show no reaction. This principle can be applied to any pair of metals: if the added metal is higher in the reactivity series than the metal in the salt, displacement occurs.

You can work out a reactivity order by doing a series of displacement experiments. Place different metals into solutions of other metal salts. If a displacement occurs (colour change, solid deposited, temperature rise), the added metal is more reactive. If nothing happens, the added metal is less reactive. By testing several combinations systematically, you can rank the metals in order of reactivity. You can also compare how vigorously different metals react with dilute acid — faster fizzing and more heat indicates higher reactivity.

Extracting Metals

How a metal is extracted from its ore depends on its position in the reactivity series. Metals below carbon in the series (such as iron, zinc and copper) can be extracted by reduction with carbon. The carbon is more reactive, so it displaces the metal from its oxide and takes the oxygen. For example, extracting iron from iron oxide:

$$2Fe_2O_3 + 3C \rightarrow 4Fe + 3CO_2$$

In this reaction, the iron oxide is reduced (loses oxygen) and the carbon is oxidised (gains oxygen). This is why carbon reduction is also a redox reaction. Metals above carbon in the series (such as aluminium, sodium and potassium) are too reactive to be extracted by carbon. They must be extracted by electrolysis, which is more expensive because it uses large amounts of electricity. For example, aluminium is extracted from aluminium oxide (bauxite) by electrolysis at around 960°C.

Biological methods offer alternatives to traditional extraction, particularly for low-grade ores where conventional mining is not economically viable. Phytoextraction uses plants to absorb metal compounds from the soil through their roots; the plants are harvested and burned, and the metal is extracted from the ash. Bioleaching uses bacteria to produce acidic solutions that dissolve metal compounds from the ore; the metal can then be extracted from the solution by displacement or electrolysis. These methods are slower but have lower environmental impact and can extract metals from ores that would otherwise be waste.

Key Fact

Metals below carbon in the reactivity series are extracted by reduction with carbon (heating the oxide with carbon). Metals above carbon must be extracted by electrolysis. The choice of method depends entirely on the metal’s reactivity relative to carbon.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For displacement reaction questions, always state which metal is more reactive and explain that the more reactive metal displaces the less reactive one. When predicting whether a reaction will occur, compare positions in the reactivity series. For metal extraction questions, explain why different methods are used for different metals — link it to the position of carbon in the series.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The reactivity series ranks metals by how easily they form positive ions. More reactive metals react more vigorously with water and acids.
  • A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a compound. Displacement experiments can be used to deduce a reactivity order.
  • Metals below carbon are extracted by reduction with carbon. Metals above carbon require electrolysis. Biological methods (phytoextraction, bioleaching) are alternatives.

lessons.title: Predicting Chemical Reactions — Groups and Trends
lessons.description: Properties of Groups 1, 7 and 0, electron arrangement and trends in reactivity.
lessons.content_html:
The Periodic Table and Groups

The modern periodic table arranges elements in order of atomic number. Elements in the same group (column) have the same number of outer-shell electrons, which is why they have similar chemical properties. Elements in the same period (row) have the same number of electron shells. Mendeleev’s original table was based on atomic mass and left gaps for undiscovered elements. His predictions about these missing elements were later confirmed, validating the periodic arrangement. The table was subsequently refined using atomic number (not atomic mass) as the fundamental organising principle, which resolved anomalies where elements would have been placed in the wrong group if ordered by mass alone.

Group 1 — The Alkali Metals

Group 1 elements (lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium, francium) are called the alkali metals. They all have one electron in their outer shell, which they lose easily to form +1 ions. They are soft metals that can be cut with a knife, have low melting points compared to most metals, and have low densities — lithium, sodium and potassium all float on water. They must be stored under oil to prevent them reacting with moisture and oxygen in the air.

Group 1 metals react with water to produce a metal hydroxide (an alkaline solution, hence “alkali metals”) and hydrogen gas. For example: \(2Na(s) + 2H_2O(l) \rightarrow 2NaOH(aq) + H_2(g)\). Lithium fizzes gently, sodium melts into a ball and fizzes vigorously, and potassium reacts so vigorously it catches fire with a lilac flame. Reactivity increases down the group because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner electrons, making it easier to lose.

Key Fact

Group 1: reactivity increases down the group because the outer electron is further from the nucleus, more shielded, so easier to lose. Melting points decrease down the group.

Group 7 — The Halogens

Group 7 elements (fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine, astatine) are called the halogens. They have seven electrons in their outer shell and need to gain one more electron to achieve a full outer shell, forming −1 ions. They exist as diatomic molecules (\(F_2\), \(Cl_2\), \(Br_2\), \(I_2\)). Halogens react with metals to form ionic compounds called halide salts (e.g. sodium chloride, NaCl) and react with non-metals to form covalent compounds.

Physical properties change down the group as the molecules get larger and intermolecular forces become stronger: fluorine is a pale yellow gas, chlorine is a green gas, bromine is a red-brown liquid, and iodine is a grey solid that sublimes to form a purple vapour. Melting and boiling points increase down the group. Reactivity decreases going down Group 7 because the outer shell is further from the nucleus, so the attraction for an incoming electron is weaker and it is harder to gain that extra electron.

A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from a solution of its salt. For example, chlorine displaces bromine from potassium bromide solution: \(Cl_2(aq) + 2KBr(aq) \rightarrow 2KCl(aq) + Br_2(aq)\). The solution changes from colourless to orange-brown as bromine is released. Similarly, chlorine displaces iodine from potassium iodide, turning the solution brown. However, bromine cannot displace chlorine from potassium chloride because bromine is less reactive than chlorine. These displacement reactions provide experimental evidence for the reactivity trend.

Group 0 — The Noble Gases

Group 0 elements (helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, radon) are the noble gases. They have full outer electron shells, which makes them very stable and unreactive. They exist as individual atoms (monatomic) rather than molecules because they have no tendency to share, gain or lose electrons. Boiling points increase down the group as the atoms become larger and intermolecular forces increase.

Noble gases are used where unreactive gases are needed: helium for balloons and airships (low density, non-flammable), neon in advertising signs (produces a distinctive red-orange glow when electricity passes through it), and argon in light bulbs and welding (prevents oxidation of the hot filament or metal).

Key Fact

Noble gases are unreactive because they have complete outer electron shells. They do not need to form bonds. Boiling points increase down the group as atomic size and intermolecular forces increase.

Going down any group, atoms have more electron shells. In Group 1, the single outer electron is progressively further from the positive nucleus and more shielded by inner electrons — so it is easier to remove (lose), making the element more reactive. In Group 7, the outer shell is further from the nucleus, so the attraction for an incoming electron is weaker — making it harder to gain an electron, so reactivity decreases. In Group 0, the full outer shell provides stability regardless of size, so all noble gases are unreactive. These trends can be explained entirely by the electronic structure of the atoms. Understanding this pattern means you can predict the properties of any element from its position in the periodic table, even if you have never studied it before.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When explaining trends in reactivity, always link your answer to electron structure. State: (1) the number of outer electrons, (2) whether the atom needs to gain or lose them, and (3) how distance from the nucleus and shielding by inner electrons affects how easily this happens. For displacement questions, state which halogen is more reactive and why, then describe the observation.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Group 1 alkali metals have 1 outer electron, react with water, and become more reactive down the group (outer electron easier to lose).
  • Group 7 halogens have 7 outer electrons, are diatomic, and become less reactive down the group (harder to attract an extra electron).
  • Group 0 noble gases have full outer shells, are unreactive, and exist as monatomic gases.

• Group 0: full outer shells → no tendency to gain or lose electrons → unreactive.

lessons.title: Identifying Substances
lessons.description: Flame tests, gas tests, and chemical analysis techniques for identifying unknown substances.
lessons.content_html:
Why We Need Chemical Tests

Chemists often need to identify unknown substances. This might be to check whether a water supply is safe, to identify minerals in rocks, to verify the purity of a manufactured product, or to analyse an unknown sample in a forensic investigation. The OCR Gateway specification requires you to know several key tests that can identify specific ions and gases. These tests fall into two broad categories: traditional wet chemistry tests that rely on visible observations, and modern instrumental methods that use machines for faster, more accurate results.

Flame Tests

A flame test identifies metal ions by the colour they produce when heated in a Bunsen burner flame. Different metal ions emit light of different colours because their electrons absorb energy and then release it as visible light at characteristic wavelengths. To carry out a flame test: dip a clean nichrome wire loop in concentrated hydrochloric acid (to remove previous residues), then dip it into the sample, and hold it in a blue Bunsen flame. The wire must be cleaned thoroughly between tests to avoid contamination from previous samples, which would give misleading results.

Key Fact

Flame test colours: Lithium — crimson red. Sodium — yellow. Potassium — lilac. Calcium — orange-red. Copper — green / blue-green.

Tests for Gases

You must be able to test for four gases. Each test produces a unique, easily identifiable result:

Hydrogen (\(H_2\)) — hold a burning splint near the mouth of the test tube; a squeaky pop confirms hydrogen. The pop is caused by the hydrogen igniting and reacting with oxygen in the air: \(2H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O\). Oxygen (\(O_2\)) — insert a glowing splint into the gas; it relights because oxygen supports combustion. Carbon dioxide (\(CO_2\)) — bubble the gas through limewater (calcium hydroxide solution); it turns milky or cloudy because insoluble calcium carbonate is formed: \(Ca(OH)_2 + CO_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3 + H_2O\). Chlorine (\(Cl_2\)) — hold damp litmus paper near the gas; it is first turned red (because chlorine is acidic) and then bleached white because chlorine is a powerful bleaching agent.

Testing for Metal Ions Using Sodium Hydroxide

Adding sodium hydroxide solution (NaOH) to solutions containing metal ions produces coloured precipitates. The precipitate forms because the metal ions react with hydroxide ions to produce an insoluble metal hydroxide. The colour of the precipitate identifies the metal ion present. This is a key practical skill for the exam.

Calcium ions (\(Ca^{2+}\)) — white precipitate of calcium hydroxide. Copper(II) ions (\(Cu^{2+}\)) — blue precipitate of copper hydroxide. Iron(II) ions (\(Fe^{2+}\)) — green precipitate of iron(II) hydroxide; the equation is \(Fe^{2+} + 2OH^- \rightarrow Fe(OH)_2\). Iron(III) ions (\(Fe^{3+}\)) — brown precipitate of iron(III) hydroxide; the equation is \(Fe^{3+} + 3OH^- \rightarrow Fe(OH)_3\). Aluminium ions (\(Al^{3+}\)) — white precipitate that dissolves in excess NaOH to form a colourless solution (aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric). Magnesium ions (\(Mg^{2+}\)) — white precipitate that does not dissolve in excess NaOH. This difference between aluminium and magnesium is important: both give white precipitates, but only aluminium’s dissolves in excess.

Testing for Negative Ions

You can test for certain negative ions (anions) using specific reagents:

Carbonate ions (\(CO_3^{2-}\)) — add dilute acid (such as hydrochloric acid) to the sample. If carbonates are present, the acid reacts to produce carbon dioxide gas, which can be tested by bubbling it through limewater — it turns milky if \(CO_2\) is present. Sulfate ions (\(SO_4^{2-}\)) — first add dilute hydrochloric acid to remove any carbonate ions that might interfere, then add barium chloride solution. A white precipitate of barium sulfate (\(BaSO_4\)) confirms sulfate ions are present. Halide ions — first add dilute nitric acid (to remove other ions that might interfere), then add silver nitrate solution. Chloride ions (\(Cl^-\)) give a white precipitate of silver chloride, bromide ions (\(Br^-\)) give a cream precipitate of silver bromide, and iodide ions (\(I^-\)) give a yellow precipitate of silver iodide.

Key Fact

Halide tests with silver nitrate: chloride \(\rightarrow\) white precipitate, bromide \(\rightarrow\) cream precipitate, iodide \(\rightarrow\) yellow precipitate. Always acidify with dilute nitric acid first to prevent interference from other ions.

When identifying an unknown ionic compound, work systematically. First dissolve the sample in water. Use a flame test to identify the metal ion (cation). Then use precipitate tests with NaOH to confirm the metal ion. Next, test for the negative ion (anion) using the appropriate reagent — silver nitrate for halides, barium chloride for sulfates, or dilute acid for carbonates. Record all observations carefully and compare with known results.

Instrumental Methods

Instrumental methods of analysis are faster, more sensitive and more accurate than traditional chemical tests. Gas chromatography separates the components of a mixture by passing it through a column; each component travels at a different rate, producing separate peaks on a chromatogram. The number of peaks tells you how many components are in the mixture, and the retention time identifies each substance. Mass spectrometry gives the relative molecular mass of a substance by measuring the mass-to-charge ratio of its ions. Gas chromatography linked with mass spectrometry (GC-MS) is particularly powerful because it both separates and identifies components in a single analysis. These methods are used in forensic science, environmental monitoring, drug testing and the pharmaceutical industry.

Instrumental methods can detect very small quantities of a substance (high sensitivity), making them invaluable when only a trace amount is available. They are fast and can be automated for processing many samples. They give accurate, quantitative results rather than just qualitative observations. However, the equipment is expensive to purchase and maintain, and requires trained operators to interpret the data correctly. Despite these costs, instrumental analysis has largely replaced traditional tests in professional laboratories.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For practical test questions, always describe the method AND the observation. For flame tests, specify the colour precisely (e.g. “crimson red” not just “red” for lithium). For precipitate tests, name the reagent added and the colour of the precipitate. If you cannot remember a specific colour, describe the observation as fully as you can.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Flame tests identify metal ions by the colour they produce: Li (crimson), Na (yellow), K (lilac), Ca (orange-red), Cu (green).
  • NaOH produces coloured precipitates with metal ions. Silver nitrate tests for halide ions (Cl⁻ white, Br⁻ cream, I⁻ yellow).
  • Gas tests: hydrogen (squeaky pop), oxygen (relights splint), CO\(_2\) (limewater turns milky), chlorine (bleaches litmus). Instrumental methods are faster and more sensitive.

lessons.title: Rates of Reaction
lessons.description: Measuring reaction rates, collision theory, and factors affecting rate of reaction.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Rate of Reaction?

The rate of reaction tells us how quickly a reaction happens — how fast the reactants are used up or how fast the products are formed. A fast reaction (like an explosion) is over in a fraction of a second. A slow reaction (like rusting or the weathering of stone) may take months or years. Being able to control the rate of a reaction is vital in industry — too fast can be dangerous, too slow is uneconomical.

You can measure rate in several ways: the volume of gas produced per unit time, the mass of reactant lost per unit time (using a balance), or the time taken for a colour change or for a solution to become opaque (disappearing cross experiment). The choice of method depends on the particular reaction and what can be conveniently measured.

Collision Theory

Collision theory states that for a reaction to occur, the reacting particles must: (1) collide with each other, (2) collide with sufficient energy (at least the activation energy), and (3) collide with the correct orientation. The rate of reaction depends on the frequency of successful collisions — collisions that have enough energy and the right orientation to result in a reaction. Not every collision leads to a reaction; most collisions are unsuccessful because the particles bounce off each other without reacting.

Key Fact

For a reaction to happen, particles must collide with enough energy (the activation energy) and the correct orientation. Increasing the frequency of successful collisions increases the rate of reaction.

Factors Affecting Rate

Four main factors affect the rate of a chemical reaction:

Temperature — increasing the temperature gives particles more kinetic energy, so they move faster and collide more frequently. More importantly, a greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or exceeding the activation energy, so the rate increases significantly.

Concentration (or pressure for gases) — increasing the concentration means there are more particles in a given volume, so they collide more frequently. For gases, increasing the pressure pushes particles closer together, having the same effect.

Surface area — breaking a solid into smaller pieces increases the surface area to volume ratio. More of the solid is exposed to the other reactant, so collisions happen more frequently and the rate increases. This is why powdered marble chips react faster with acid than large lumps, even though the total mass of marble is the same. In the extreme case, a fine powder of a combustible material in air can cause a dust explosion because the surface area is so enormous that the reaction rate is dangerously fast.

Interpreting Rate of Reaction Graphs

Rate graphs typically plot volume of gas produced (or mass lost) on the y-axis against time on the x-axis. The gradient (steepness) of the line shows the rate — a steeper gradient means a faster reaction. The line levels off when one of the reactants is used up (the reaction is complete). The final amount of product is the same regardless of rate (unless the amount of reactant changes). Two curves on the same graph — one steep and one gradual — that level off at the same point indicate the same amount of reactant was used but one reaction was faster than the other.

You can also use \(\frac{1}{t}\) as a measure of rate, where \(t\) is the time taken for a certain amount of reaction to occur. A shorter time means a faster rate, so \(\frac{1}{t}\) is proportional to rate.

Catalysts

A catalyst is a substance that increases the rate of a reaction without being used up itself. It works by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so more particles have enough energy to react. On a reaction profile, the catalyst lowers the energy barrier (the peak). The catalyst itself is unchanged at the end of the reaction and can be reused. Each catalyst is specific to a particular reaction or type of reaction — an iron catalyst works for the Haber process but not for decomposing hydrogen peroxide (which uses manganese dioxide).

Key Fact

Catalysts speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy. They are not used up and are not changed permanently. Different reactions need different catalysts. Enzymes are biological catalysts that control reactions in living organisms.

Gas syringe method: collect gas produced in a gas syringe and record the volume at regular time intervals. Works well for reactions producing \(CO_2\) or \(H_2\) (e.g. marble chips and acid, magnesium and acid). Mass loss method: place the reaction on a balance and record the mass at regular intervals as gas escapes. Disappearing cross: time how long it takes for a cross viewed through the solution to disappear as the solution becomes opaque (sodium thiosulfate and acid producing sulfur). In all methods, change only one variable at a time and keep everything else constant.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When interpreting rate graphs, describe the gradient (“steep at first, then levels off”) and explain what each part shows. For catalyst questions on reaction profiles, draw a dotted line showing the lower activation energy peak — the overall energy change stays the same. Always specify that a catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy rather than just saying it “speeds up” the reaction.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Rate depends on the frequency of successful collisions. Factors: temperature (more energy), concentration/pressure (more particles), surface area (more exposure).
  • Rate graphs show volume or mass against time. Steeper gradient = faster rate. The line levels off when the reaction is complete.
  • Catalysts lower the activation energy by providing an alternative pathway. They are not used up. Enzymes are biological catalysts.

lessons.title: Equilibria
lessons.description: Reversible reactions, dynamic equilibrium, and Le Chatelier's principle.
lessons.content_html:
Reversible Reactions

Most chemical reactions go to completion — the reactants are used up and only products remain. However, some reactions are reversible. In a reversible reaction, the products can react to re-form the original reactants. This is shown by the equilibrium symbol \(\rightleftharpoons\) instead of a single arrow. Many important industrial and biological reactions are reversible, and understanding how to control them is essential for maximising product yield in chemical manufacturing.

For example, the decomposition of ammonium chloride: \(NH_4Cl(s) \rightleftharpoons NH_3(g) + HCl(g)\). When heated, ammonium chloride breaks down into ammonia and hydrogen chloride gases. When cooled, these gases recombine to form solid ammonium chloride again. The forward reaction is endothermic (absorbs energy); the reverse reaction is exothermic (releases energy). Another example is the reaction of hydrated copper sulfate: blue \(CuSO_4 \cdot 5H_2O\) turns white (anhydrous \(CuSO_4\)) when heated, and turns blue again when water is added.

Key Fact

In a reversible reaction, if the forward reaction is exothermic, the reverse reaction is endothermic (and vice versa). The energy change in each direction has the same magnitude but opposite sign.

Dynamic Equilibrium

When a reversible reaction takes place in a closed system (where nothing can enter or leave), a dynamic equilibrium is eventually reached. At equilibrium, three conditions are met:

• The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction.

• The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant (but not necessarily equal to each other).

• Both reactions are still occurring at the molecular level — this is why it is called “dynamic.” Molecules are continuously reacting in both directions, but the overall proportions do not change.

Equilibrium does not mean the amounts of reactants and products are equal — it means they are constant. The equilibrium position can favour the products (more products than reactants) or the reactants (more reactants than products). Also, equilibrium is not a static state — both reactions continue at equal rates, like two escalators running in opposite directions at the same speed. You can only achieve equilibrium in a closed system; in an open system, products can escape and equilibrium is never reached.

Le Chatelier’s Principle (Higher)

Le Chatelier’s principle states that if the conditions of a system at equilibrium are changed, the equilibrium position shifts to oppose the change and partially counteract it. This principle allows us to predict which direction the equilibrium will move when we alter temperature, concentration or pressure.

Temperature: Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction (to absorb the extra heat and reduce the temperature). Decreasing temperature favours the exothermic direction. This changes both the rate and the equilibrium position. Concentration: Increasing the concentration of a reactant shifts equilibrium towards the products (to use up the extra reactant). Increasing the concentration of a product shifts equilibrium towards the reactants. Removing a product also shifts the equilibrium to the right. Pressure (for reactions involving gases): Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules (to reduce the pressure). Decreasing pressure favours the side with more gas molecules. Count the total moles of gas on each side to predict the shift.

A catalyst does not change the equilibrium position — it speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but the final proportions of reactants and products are unchanged. This is an important distinction that is frequently tested.

The Haber Process

The Haber process is the most important industrial example of Le Chatelier’s principle in action. It produces ammonia, which is essential for making fertilisers, explosives and cleaning products. The equation is:

$$N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)$$

The forward reaction is exothermic (\(\Delta H = -92\) kJ/mol). There are 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 moles on the right. Applying Le Chatelier’s principle: a low temperature would favour the exothermic (forward) direction and increase yield, but the rate would be unacceptably slow. A high pressure would favour the side with fewer moles of gas (the products), increasing yield, but very high pressures are dangerous and expensive. Industrial conditions are therefore a compromise: temperature of about 450°C (high enough for a reasonable rate), pressure of about 200 atm (high enough for a good yield without excessive cost), and an iron catalyst (speeds up the reaction so equilibrium is reached faster without changing the position). Unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled back through the reactor to maximise efficiency, meaning that even though the percentage conversion per pass is only about 15%, the overall yield is much higher over time. Ammonia is a crucial chemical: it is used to make ammonium nitrate fertiliser, nitric acid, and various cleaning products.

Key Fact

Haber process: \(N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3\). Conditions: ~450°C, ~200 atm, iron catalyst. These are a compromise between yield and rate of reaction. Unreacted gases are recycled.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When applying Le Chatelier’s principle, state the change, the direction the equilibrium shifts, and why (to oppose the change). For the Haber process, always explain that the conditions are a compromise — the word “compromise” is essential for full marks. Remember: a catalyst does not shift the equilibrium position.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Reversible reactions can go in both directions. Dynamic equilibrium is reached in a closed system when the forward and reverse rates are equal.
  • Le Chatelier’s principle: changing temperature, concentration or pressure shifts the equilibrium to oppose the change. Catalysts do not change the equilibrium position.
  • The Haber process makes ammonia at ~450°C, ~200 atm with an iron catalyst — a compromise between yield and rate.

lessons.title: Improving Processes and Products
lessons.description: Metal extraction, life cycle assessments, crude oil fractions and cracking.
lessons.content_html:
Atom Economy and Percentage Yield

In industrial chemistry, it is not enough to simply make a product — the process must be efficient and produce as little waste as possible. Two key measures of efficiency are atom economy and percentage yield.

Atom economy measures how much of the mass of the reactants ends up as the useful product. A high atom economy means less waste is produced, which is better for both the environment and the company’s costs. It is calculated using:

$$\text{atom economy} = \frac{M_r \text{ of desired product}}{\text{sum of } M_r \text{ of all products}} \times 100$$

Percentage yield compares the actual amount of product obtained to the maximum theoretical amount (from the balanced equation):

$$\text{percentage yield} = \frac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}} \times 100$$

Percentage yield is often less than 100% because of incomplete reactions, side reactions, product lost during purification, or reversible reactions that do not go to completion. The limiting reactant is the one that runs out first and determines the maximum amount of product that can be formed. The other reactant is said to be in excess — some of it will be left over when the reaction finishes. For example, if you react 2 g of magnesium with 100 cm³ of excess hydrochloric acid, the magnesium is the limiting reactant and determines how much hydrogen is produced.

Key Fact

Atom economy measures the proportion of reactant atoms that become the desired product. Percentage yield measures how much product was actually made compared to the theoretical maximum. Both should be as high as possible for economic and environmental reasons. Industry aims for reactions with 100% atom economy (where all atoms end up in the desired product), but this is not always achievable, especially in reactions that produce by-products.

Life Cycle Assessments

A life cycle assessment (LCA) evaluates the environmental impact of a product at every stage of its life. The four main stages are: (1) extracting and processing raw materials, (2) manufacturing the product, (3) using the product (including transport), and (4) disposing of the product at the end of its life.

LCAs consider: energy consumption at each stage, raw material use, water use, emissions to air (including greenhouse gases), emissions to water, waste produced, and the potential for recycling or reuse. However, some aspects are difficult to quantify (e.g. the impact of noise pollution or visual impact), which makes LCAs partly subjective. Different analysts may reach different conclusions depending on the weighting they give to different factors. Companies may also use LCAs selectively to support marketing claims, so it is important to evaluate LCA data critically.

Recycling

Recycling materials reduces the need to extract new raw materials, saves energy, and reduces waste going to landfill. Factors affecting recycling decisions include: the cost of collection and processing, the value of the recycled material, the energy savings compared to making new material, and public willingness to recycle. Metals such as aluminium are particularly worth recycling because extracting aluminium from bauxite by electrolysis is very energy-intensive — recycling aluminium uses only about 5% of the energy needed to extract it from ore. Glass, paper and many plastics can also be recycled, though the economics depend on collection costs, sorting complexity and the market value of recycled material.

Crude Oil and Hydrocarbons

Crude oil is a finite resource and a vital feedstock for the petrochemical industry. It is a complex mixture of hundreds of different hydrocarbons — mostly alkanes, which have the general formula \(C_nH_{2n+2}\). Crude oil is separated into useful fractions by fractional distillation. The oil is heated and vapours rise up a fractionating column; fractions with lower boiling points (shorter molecules with weaker intermolecular forces) are collected near the top, and those with higher boiling points (longer molecules with stronger intermolecular forces) near the bottom. The main fractions include refinery gases, petrol (gasoline), kerosene, diesel, fuel oil and bitumen.

Cracking breaks long-chain hydrocarbons (which are less useful) into shorter, more useful molecules. There is high demand for short-chain hydrocarbons (for fuels) and for alkenes (used to make polymers). Cracking can be done by passing hydrocarbon vapour over a hot catalyst (catalytic cracking) or by mixing with steam at very high temperatures (steam cracking). The products include shorter alkanes (used as fuels like petrol and diesel) and alkenes (unsaturated hydrocarbons used as the starting materials for making polymers such as polyethylene and polypropylene). The general equation for cracking might look like: \(C_{10}H_{22} \rightarrow C_8H_{18} + C_2H_4\), where a long-chain alkane is split into a shorter alkane and an alkene.

Key Fact

Crude oil is a finite resource and a vital feedstock for the petrochemical industry. It is separated by fractional distillation based on boiling point. Long-chain hydrocarbons are cracked to produce shorter, more useful alkanes (fuels) and alkenes (for making polymers). Modern life is crucially dependent on hydrocarbons for energy, transport and materials.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For LCA questions, think about all four stages of a product’s life and mention specific environmental impacts (energy use, emissions, waste). For atom economy calculations, make sure you use the \(M_r\) of the desired product only on top, and the \(M_r\) of all products on the bottom. For questions on crude oil, distinguish between fractional distillation (physical separation) and cracking (chemical process).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Atom economy measures waste efficiency; percentage yield measures how much product is actually obtained. Both should be maximised.
  • Life cycle assessments evaluate environmental impact from raw materials to disposal. Recycling reduces resource use and energy consumption.
  • Crude oil is separated by fractional distillation. Cracking converts long-chain hydrocarbons into shorter alkanes (fuels) and alkenes (for polymers).

lessons.title: Earth's Atmosphere and Climate
lessons.description: Atmospheric composition over time, greenhouse effect, and human impact on climate.
lessons.content_html:
The Current Atmosphere

The Earth’s atmosphere today is approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and about 1% other gases including argon (about 0.9%), carbon dioxide (about 0.04%), and small amounts of water vapour. This composition has been relatively stable for about 200 million years, though human activities are now causing measurable changes to the concentrations of certain gases, particularly carbon dioxide and methane. Understanding how and why the atmosphere has changed is essential for evaluating the evidence around climate change.

How the Atmosphere Evolved

The atmosphere has changed dramatically over Earth’s 4.6-billion-year history. Scientists believe the early atmosphere was formed by intense volcanic activity during the first billion years. It was very different from today: it consisted mainly of carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen, along with water vapour and small amounts of methane and ammonia — similar to the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today. As the Earth cooled, water vapour condensed to form the oceans, and some carbon dioxide dissolved in this water. The evidence for the early atmosphere comes from analysis of ancient rocks, volcanic emissions, and comparison with other planets in our solar system.

About 2.7 billion years ago, early organisms that could photosynthesise (including algae and cyanobacteria) evolved in the oceans. Photosynthesis absorbed carbon dioxide and released oxygen: \(6CO_2 + 6H_2O \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2\). Over hundreds of millions of years, this gradually increased the oxygen level and decreased the carbon dioxide level. As oxygen accumulated, it formed the ozone layer (\(O_3\)) in the upper atmosphere, which blocked harmful ultraviolet radiation and allowed life to move onto land. Some carbon dioxide also dissolved in the oceans, was used by marine organisms to make calcium carbonate shells, and was eventually locked away in sedimentary rocks (limestone) and fossil fuels.

Key Fact

The early atmosphere was mainly \(CO_2\) from volcanoes. Photosynthesis by early organisms increased oxygen and decreased carbon dioxide over billions of years. Carbon dioxide was also dissolved in oceans and locked in sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels.

The Greenhouse Effect

The greenhouse effect is a natural process that keeps the Earth warm enough to support life. Without it, the average surface temperature would be about −18°C instead of about 15°C. Short-wavelength radiation from the Sun passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth’s surface. The warm surface emits longer-wavelength infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour) absorb some of this infrared radiation and re-emit it in all directions, including back towards Earth. This traps heat energy in the atmosphere and keeps the surface warmer than it would otherwise be. The greenhouse effect is essential for life on Earth, but problems arise when human activities increase the concentration of these gases beyond natural levels.

Climate Change

Human activities are increasing the concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, enhancing the natural greenhouse effect. Burning fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) releases carbon dioxide that was locked away millions of years ago. Deforestation reduces the number of trees absorbing \(CO_2\) by photosynthesis. Agriculture (especially cattle farming and rice paddies) produces methane. Landfill sites also release methane as waste decomposes. The increase in greenhouse gases is enhancing the greenhouse effect, leading to global warming and climate change.

There is a strong correlation between increased fossil fuel use, rising atmospheric \(CO_2\) levels and rising global temperatures. Ice core data from Antarctica and Greenland shows that \(CO_2\) levels today are higher than at any point in the last 800,000 years. The rate of increase is also unprecedented. However, there are uncertainties in the evidence: climate models are complex and depend on many variables, natural climate variations (such as volcanic eruptions and solar cycles) also occur, and the exact extent and timing of future warming is debated. Despite these uncertainties, the scientific consensus — supported by organisations like the IPCC — is that human activities are the dominant cause of recent warming.

Potential Effects and Mitigation

Potential effects of climate change include: rising sea levels (from melting ice caps and thermal expansion of warmer ocean water), more frequent and intense extreme weather events (storms, floods, droughts, heatwaves), changes to rainfall patterns affecting agriculture, loss of biodiversity as habitats change faster than species can adapt, and disruption to food production, and displacement of populations in low-lying coastal areas. Mitigation strategies include: reducing fossil fuel use, increasing use of renewable energy (solar, wind, hydroelectric), carbon capture and storage technology, improving energy efficiency in buildings and transport, reforestation to absorb more \(CO_2\), and international agreements to limit emissions. Individual actions such as reducing energy use, using public transport, and reducing meat consumption also contribute.

Key Fact

Human activities (burning fossil fuels, deforestation, agriculture) are increasing greenhouse gas levels. This enhances the greenhouse effect, causing global warming and climate change. There is strong evidence for this but some uncertainties remain in predictions about the scale and timing of future impacts.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For “describe” questions on the evolution of the atmosphere, present the stages in chronological order and link each change to a cause. For climate change “evaluate” questions, discuss both the evidence (ice cores, temperature data, correlation with fossil fuel use) and the limitations of that evidence (models, natural variation). Always distinguish between the natural greenhouse effect (essential for life) and the enhanced greenhouse effect (caused by human activity).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The early atmosphere was mainly \(CO_2\) from volcanoes. Photosynthesis increased oxygen and decreased \(CO_2\) over billions of years.
  • The greenhouse effect is natural and essential, but human activities are enhancing it by increasing \(CO_2\) and methane levels.
  • Climate change effects include rising sea levels, extreme weather and biodiversity loss. Mitigation includes renewables, efficiency and reforestation.

lessons.title: Earth's Resources and Sustainability
lessons.description: Potable water, pollution, sustainable development and recycling materials.
lessons.content_html:
Finite and Renewable Resources

The Earth provides natural resources that humans depend on. Finite resources (also called non-renewable) will eventually run out because they are consumed faster than they form. Examples include fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas), which took millions of years to form from the remains of ancient organisms, and metal ores mined from the Earth’s crust. Renewable resources can be replaced at the same rate they are used — examples include wood (from managed forests), crops, wind energy, solar energy and hydroelectric power.

Sustainable development means meeting the needs of the current population without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. This requires careful management of resources, reducing waste, recycling materials, developing alternatives to finite resources, and ensuring that the environmental costs of production are minimised at every stage. Chemistry plays a central role in sustainable development — from designing industrial processes with higher atom economy and lower waste to developing biodegradable materials, more efficient batteries, and renewable energy technologies such as hydrogen fuel cells.

Key Fact

Sustainable development requires using resources wisely so that future generations can meet their needs. This involves reducing consumption of finite resources, recycling, and developing renewable alternatives.

Potable Water

Potable water is water that is safe to drink. It is not pure in the chemical sense (it still contains dissolved substances such as mineral salts) but has sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts and harmful microbes to be safe for human consumption. The UK is fortunate to have abundant fresh water from rivers, lakes and reservoirs. Potable water is produced from these sources by a multi-stage process that involves:

Step 1: Filtration — passing the water through filter beds (sand and gravel) to remove solid particles and debris. Step 2: Sterilisation — killing harmful bacteria and microorganisms. This can be done using chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet (UV) light. Chlorine is most commonly used in the UK because it is effective, cheap, and continues to kill bacteria as the water travels through the distribution network.

In areas with limited fresh water, sea water or brackish water (slightly salty water) can be made potable by desalination. This can be done by distillation (boiling and condensing) or by reverse osmosis (forcing water through a membrane that blocks dissolved salts). Desalination requires large amounts of energy, making it expensive. In the UK, where rainfall is generally sufficient, fresh water treatment is more cost-effective. In arid countries like Saudi Arabia or the UAE, desalination is essential despite the high energy cost.

Treating Waste Water

Waste water (from homes, industry and agriculture) must be treated before being released back into the environment. Sewage treatment is a multi-stage process: screening and grit removal (removing large solids and debris), primary sedimentation (allowing smaller solids to settle as sludge in settlement tanks), biological treatment (aerobic microorganisms break down dissolved organic matter in aeration tanks), secondary sedimentation, and final filtration and sterilisation before the clean effluent is returned to rivers. Industrial waste water may also contain harmful chemicals such as heavy metals or toxic organic compounds that require specialised treatment before the water can be safely released. Agricultural run-off containing fertilisers can cause eutrophication in waterways if not properly managed.

Atmospheric Pollutants

The combustion of fossil fuels produces several harmful pollutants that damage human health and the environment. You need to know the source, identity and effects of each one:

Carbon monoxide (CO) — produced by incomplete combustion of fuels. It is a toxic, colourless, odourless gas that reduces the blood’s ability to carry oxygen by binding to haemoglobin. Sulfur dioxide (\(SO_2\)) — produced when fossil fuels containing sulfur impurities are burned. It causes acid rain, which damages buildings, harms aquatic life and kills plants. Oxides of nitrogen (\(NO_x\)) — produced at high temperatures in car engines when nitrogen and oxygen from the air react. They also cause acid rain and contribute to smog. Particulates (tiny solid particles, including soot) — produced by incomplete combustion. They cause respiratory problems, reduced visibility, and can contribute to climate change.

Key Fact

Burning fossil fuels produces: carbon monoxide (toxic gas, incomplete combustion), sulfur dioxide (acid rain), oxides of nitrogen (acid rain, smog), and particulates (respiratory problems). These pollutants have serious health and environmental impacts.

Reducing Pollution

Pollution from combustion can be reduced by: using catalytic converters in vehicles (which convert CO and \(NO_x\) to less harmful \(CO_2\) and \(N_2\)), removing sulfur from fuels before burning, using flue gas desulfurisation in power stations, switching to renewable energy sources, and improving engine efficiency. Switching to electric vehicles reduces exhaust emissions at the point of use, though the overall environmental benefit depends on how the electricity is generated. These strategies involve balancing environmental benefits against economic costs technological feasibility, and public willingness to change behaviour.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For water treatment questions, be specific: state the separation techniques used (filtration, sterilisation) and name the sterilising agent (chlorine, ozone or UV). For desalination, mention that it requires large amounts of energy — this is why it is not used everywhere. For pollutant questions, always link each pollutant to its source AND its effect on health or the environment.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Finite resources will run out; renewable resources can be replenished. Sustainable development balances current needs with future generations’ needs.
  • Potable water is made by filtration and sterilisation. Desalination can treat sea water but requires a lot of energy.
  • Fossil fuel combustion produces pollutants: CO (toxic), \(SO_2\) (acid rain), \(NO_x\) (acid rain, smog), particulates (respiratory problems). These can be reduced by catalytic converters, cleaner fuels and renewables.
